lesson.title: Lesson plan: {hub}
lesson.footer: Made with the Saving Planets Lesson Plan Builder. Free to copy and adapt for your class.

step.hookText: Share an Amazing Fact below and ask: what surprised you?
step.exploreText: Look at these solution pages together:
step.wrapText: Use the discussion questions, then the exit ticket.

questions: How does {sol} help both people and nature?
If you could ask the team behind {sol} one question, what would it be?

k3.label: K-3 (ages 5-8)
objectives: Name one way people help {hub} that is also good for nature.
Tell a friend one wow fact about {hub}.
Draw how people and animals both benefit.
materials: Screen or printouts of the solution page
k3.activity: Wow circle: read the fact aloud, then each child draws the helper (a person, an animal or a machine) and shares it.
k3.exit: Draw or say one way you could help {hub}.

g45.label: Grades 4-5
objectives: Describe a problem in {hub} and one solution that is working now.
Explain how the solution helps both people and nature.
Use two new vocabulary words correctly.
materials: Screens or printouts of the solution pages
Five W’s chart (who, what, when, where, why)
g45.activity: Solution detectives: in pairs, read one solution page and fill in the Five W’s, then share one surprise with the class.
g45.exit: Write one thing you learned and one question you still have.

g68.label: Grades 6-8
objectives: Compare two {hub} solutions: who runs them, what they do and where.
Support a claim with evidence from a cited source.
Explain the trade-offs of each solution for people and for nature.
materials: Screens or printouts of the solution pages
T-chart: benefits for people / benefits for nature
g68.activity: Compare and contrast: groups take two solution pages and build a T-chart of benefits for people and for nature, then rank which helps more and why.
g68.exit: Write a claim about {hub} and one piece of evidence that supports it.

g912.label: Grades 9-12
objectives: Evaluate the evidence behind a {hub} solution using its original sources.
Analyze how science, technology and policy combine in the solution.
Propose an improvement that benefits both people and nature.
materials: Source-evaluation checklist (who published it, when, what evidence)
g912.activity: Source check: groups trace one Amazing Fact to its original source, judge how strong the evidence is, and present a one-minute verdict.
g912.exit: In two sentences: which source was strongest, and why?

uni.label: University
objectives: Critically assess the published evidence for {hub} solutions and its limits.
Map the stakeholders, funding and governance behind one solution.
Design a monitoring or research question with measurable outcomes for people and nature.
materials: Devices with internet and library database access
Original reports and papers linked from each solution page
uni.activity: Seminar brief: each student writes a one-page brief on one solution: the evidence, the open questions, and how success could be measured for people and nature. Peer-review in pairs.
uni.exit: Submit one research question about {hub} and the data you would need to answer it.

Earth_Observation.html.name: Earth Observation
Earth_Observation.html.blurb: Satellites are like eyes in the sky. They watch forests, ice, air and oceans so we can protect them.

sols.d: JAXA's DAICHI-4 radar sees through clouds over a 200 km swath, continuing the radar record used for deforestation alerts.
ESA's Biomass satellite launched on April 29, 2025 on Vega-C. ESA (European Space Agency). The first P-band synthetic aperture radar in space.
Sentinel-1 radar sees through clouds, day and night, to map floods, earthquakes and ice; Sentinel-1C and 1D joined in 2024 and 2025.
Sentinel-2C joined the Copernicus fleet in September 2024, imaging land and coasts in 13 bands so forests and crops are checked every five days.
From geostationary orbit on MTG-S1, Sentinel-4 measures air pollution over Europe and North Africa every hour (ESA).
Sentinel-6B, launched November 17, 2025, continues the precise record of global sea level that began in the early 1990s.
A camera photographing the entire sunlit face of Earth several times a day.
ESA–JAXA EarthCARE carries the first space cloud radar that can measure how cloud particles move up and down.
India's EOS-06, the third Oceansat, tracks ocean color, sea-surface temperature and winds; it imaged Cyclone Mandous and an algal bloom on day one.
Launched together on September 15, 2026, ESA's FLEX maps the faint glow of photosynthesis while Sentinel-3C watches oceans and land.
JAXA's IBUKI GW tracks carbon dioxide, methane and nitrogen dioxide while also measuring the water cycle.
Twin US-German satellites weigh Earth's water by measuring gravity, tracking groundwater, ice and sea level since 2018. Active.
NASA's ICESat-2 laser fires 10,000 pulses a second to measure ice sheets, sea ice, forests and coastal seafloor in 3D. Active.
Landsat 9 continues a 50-year record of Earth’s land, collecting 740 scenes a day and, with Landsat 8, seeing each place every 8 days.
Launched August 2025 on Ariane 6, MetOp-SG-A1 carries Sentinel-5, which delivers daily global data on air pollutants, ozone and climate gases.
NISAR launched from India on July 30, 2025. NASA and ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation).
NASA's PACE reads the color of the ocean to track phytoplankton, the base of the marine food web, plus aerosols and clouds.
Satellites that detect signals from emergency beacons on boats, planes and hikers and relay their location.
SWOT measures more than 95% of Earth's lakes larger than 15 acres and rivers wider than 330 feet, the first global survey of fresh water.
Tanager-1 was built by Planet with a NASA JPL-designed imaging spectrometer for the nonprofit Carbon Mapper coalition.
From geostationary orbit, NASA's TEMPO measures air pollution over North America every daylight hour, a first from space (NASA).
A chain of sensors that measures the ocean itself, not just the shaking ground, so forecasters can confirm a tsunami and estimate its size.

facts.x: EarthCARE carries the first cloud radar in space that can measure how fast cloud particles move up and down.
facts.sn: JAXA, EarthCARE Cloud Profiling Radar

facts.x: ICESat-2's laser fires 10,000 pulses a second, each with about 300 trillion photons, and only about a dozen return to the satellite.
facts.sn: NASA, ICESat-2

facts.x: Satellites listening for emergency beacons helped rescue 300 people in and around the U.S. in 2025.
facts.sn: NOAA, NOAA satellites helped rescue 300 people in 2025

facts.x: NASA–CNES SWOT keeps watch on the water levels of more than a million lakes larger than 15 acres.
facts.sn: NASA Earthdata, SWOT data release

facts.x: Sentinel-4 watches Europe's air pollution every hour from 36,000 km up.
facts.sn: ESA, Sentinel-4 offers first glimpses of air pollutants

facts.x: NASA's TEMPO checks North America's air pollution every daylight hour from 22,000 miles up.
facts.sn: NASA, TEMPO instrument launches

facts.x: About 70 minutes after the 2025 Kamchatka earthquake, the SWOT satellite measured the tsunami from space: a wave more than 1.5 feet high racing across the Pacific.
facts.sn: NASA, SWOT satellite measures tsunami after massive quake

terms.d: A tool that sends out radio waves and listens for the echoes. From space it can see the ground through clouds, day or night.
A series of giant ocean waves, usually caused by an undersea earthquake, volcano or landslide.
The total amount of living material, like the wood and leaves in a forest. Measuring it shows how much carbon plants store.
The curved path an object takes as it travels around a planet, moon or star, like a satellite circling Earth.
A gas high in the sky that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun. Near the ground, ozone is a pollutant.
A gas, like carbon dioxide or methane, that traps heat in the air around Earth, the way a greenhouse keeps plants warm.
A greenhouse gas that traps much more heat than carbon dioxide over a few decades. It leaks from oil and gas sites, landfills and farms.
Tiny bits of dust, smoke, salt or pollution floating in the air. They can block sunlight and help clouds form.
A high orbit, about 22,000 miles up, where a satellite moves with Earth's spin and stays over the same spot.
Tiny plant-like living things that drift in water and use sunlight to make food. They make much of the oxygen we breathe and feed ocean life.
A community of living things and the place they live, like a reef or a forest, all depending on each other.
A kind of light our eyes can't see that we feel as heat. Special cameras use it to see warm objects and gases.

Deforestation.html.name: Forests
Deforestation.html.blurb: Forests are homes for animals and help keep our air clean. People are planting trees and protecting wild places.

sols.d: A free online map with forest data, weekly deforestation alerts and a field app called Forest Watcher.
A mosaic of restored land, trees, farms and pastures stretching across Africa.
Rainwater harvesting with "Earth Smile" bunds and regrowing trees from old stumps (farmer managed natural regeneration).

Community-based tree planting paired with an app and monitoring technology that registers every tree and tracks its growth. They run large professional plantings, local volunteer events, school climate education, and corporate tree-adoption programs.
About 80 species of mangrove trees guard tropical coastlines, holding mud in place and softening storm surges.
Since 2014, One Tree Planted has planted more than 171 million trees with 489 partners in 84 countries (organization figure).
Solar-powered Guardian devices high in trees that listen to the forest and use AI to spot threats.
Rewilding Europe helps wild nature come back across Europe.
Every year about 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust falls on the Amazon, delivering some 22,000 tons of phosphorus that the rainforest needs (NASA).
Terraformation restores native, biodiverse forests from seed to canopy across the tropics and Hawaii.

sols.t: The Amazon Makes Its Own Rainy Season
sols.d: Water breathed out by Amazon trees starts the rainy season two to three months before winds alone would bring it (NASA JPL).

sols.t: Three Trees for Every One Removed
sols.d: For every tree removed, three go back in — rebuilding habitat, soil, and shade. A forest solution on Saving Planets.
Partnering with East African farmers on regenerative farms: 450M+ trees grown and 99,000 acres restored (nonprofit figures).

facts.x: Amazon trees start their own rainy season two to three months before the ocean-driven rains arrive.
facts.sn: NASA JPL, the Amazon makes its own rainy season

facts.x: Where Indigenous monitors used Global Forest Watch data, deforestation fell 52% in a year.
facts.sn: Global Forest Watch (now Global Nature Watch), Our History

facts.x: African countries are working to restore a band of land across the Sahel, south of the Sahara.
facts.sn: UNCCD, First Great Green Wall status report

facts.x: Justdiggit digs smile-shaped pits that catch rain and turn dry land green.
facts.sn: Justdiggit, Our impact

facts.x: There are about 80 species of mangrove trees, and their tangled roots help shield coastlines from storm surges.
facts.sn: NOAA, What is a mangrove forest?

facts.x: One Tree Planted and its partners have planted more than 171 million trees in 84 countries.
facts.sn: One Tree Planted, About Us

facts.x: Rainforest Connection hides solar-powered listening devices in trees to hear illegal logging as it happens.
facts.sn: Rainforest Connection

facts.x: Wild European bison, Europe's largest land mammal, grew from about 2,500 to 7,000 in 10 years.
facts.sn: Rewilding Europe

facts.x: About 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust fall on the Amazon each year, enough to fill 104,908 semi trucks.
facts.sn: NASA, Saharan dust feeds the Amazon

terms.d: A tree that grows in salty water along tropical coasts. Its tangled roots protect shores from waves and shelter young fish.
The variety of all living things in a place: plants, animals, fungi and tiny microbes.
Planting trees where a forest was lost so it can grow back.
The total amount of living material, like the wood and leaves in a forest. Measuring it shows how much carbon plants store.
A community of living things and the place they live, like a reef or a forest, all depending on each other.
Large brown seaweed that grows in cool ocean water and forms underwater forests full of sea life.
A coastal wetland of grasses that floods with salty tide water. It soaks up storm surges and stores carbon in its mud.
Flowering plants that grow underwater in shallow seas, forming meadows that shelter animals and store carbon.

Lakes.html.name: Lakes
Lakes.html.blurb: Lakes hold fresh water for animals and people. Divers and robots are pulling trash out of them.

sols.d: Beach cleanups where volunteers pick up litter and record what they find.
Clean Up the Lake removes submerged litter from freshwater lakes using scuba divers and community volunteers.
The Great Lakes Plastic Cleanup captures plastic across the world's largest freshwater system using Seabins, drones, and beach robots.

sols.t: Lake Erie Harmful Algal Bloom Forecast (NOAA)
sols.d: NOAA forecasts and tracks toxic algae in western Lake Erie through the summer so cities and swimmers can keep drinking water and people safe (NOAA NCCOS).
Lake Plastic Recovery: pulling plastic out of lakes before it moves downstream. A freshwater solution on Saving Planets.
A Nevada nonprofit using ROVs and volunteer divers to remove submerged debris from Lake Tahoe's depths.

facts.x: About 85% of the litter Adopt-a-Beach volunteers pick up on Great Lakes beaches is plastic.
facts.sn: Alliance for the Great Lakes, Adopt-a-Beach

facts.x: NOAA forecasts toxic algae on Lake Erie the way meteorologists forecast storms.
facts.sn: NOAA NCCOS, Timely toxin data helped Ohio deliver safe drinking water

terms.d: When tiny water plants called algae grow out of control. Some make toxins that can harm people, pets and fish.
A community of living things and the place they live, like a reef or a forest, all depending on each other.
Pieces of plastic smaller than 5 millimeters, about the size of a grain of rice or smaller. They come from bigger plastic breaking apart.

Oceans.html.name: Oceans
Oceans.html.blurb: The ocean covers most of our planet. People are cleaning up plastic and growing sea gardens so fish, turtles and people all stay healthy.

sols.d: 4ocean removes plastic from oceans, rivers, and coastlines with full-time cleanup crews, funded by products made from recovered plastic.
A New York nonprofit restoring the harbor with oyster reefs, aiming for one billion oysters by 2030 (nonprofit figures).
Growing coral fragments in nurseries and replanting them on damaged reefs, using new tools and methods.
Collecting coral eggs and sperm during spawning and rearing baby corals in floating pools and tanks before placing them on damaged reefs.
Coral Restoration Foundation had returned 253,833 corals to Florida's reefs by the end of 2024 (organization figure).
Free public maps and data that show where boats fish, built from vessel GPS signals, satellite images and machine learning.
Volunteer divers recover ghost nets: Healthy Seas reports 1,309.1 tons of nets and marine litter removed since 2013 (Healthy Seas figure).
Kelp can grow up to 18 inches a day, building underwater forests that feed and shelter thousands of species.
Mote scientists have restored more than 216,000 corals to Florida's Coral Reef, and their restored corals now spawn (Mote figure).
A sailing nonprofit that has pulled more than 850,000 pounds of plastic from the Pacific Gyre in 10 voyages (nonprofit figure).
Tiny ocean plants produce about half of Earth's oxygen, making phytoplankton one of the planet's most important natural systems.
Plastic Bank turns ocean-bound plastic into income for collectors in vulnerable communities. Making plastic worth collecting before it reaches the ocean.
The Mediterranean seagrass Posidonia oceanica forms meadows that are thousands of years old and store carbon in the seafloor (CEAB-CSIC).
Project Seagrass, a UK charity, has planted more than 150,000 seagrass seeds to bring back underwater meadows (organization figures).
Salt marshes are nurseries for more than 75% of fisheries species and buffer shorelines from erosion and floods (NOAA).
Seabin's floating bins have captured 33.0 million items in Sydney Harbour since 2020, including 18.9 million microplastics (company figures).
Seagrass covers just 0.1% of the seafloor but stores 11% of the ocean's buried organic carbon. See also Mangroves on Deforestation.
The Ocean Cleanup removes plastic from oceans and intercepts it in rivers. The largest cleanup in history — removing plastic from our oceans and rivers.
Whale waste carries nutrients to the ocean surface and fertilizes phytoplankton, the tiny plants at the base of the ocean food web (NOAA Fisheries).

Planetary_Defense.html.name: Planetary Defense
Planetary_Defense.html.blurb: Scientists watch the sky for space rocks. A NASA spacecraft called DART even nudged an asteroid to show we can move one!

sols.d: Three spacecraft will wait in space for a fresh comet and fly past it together to make a 3D map; launch is planned for late 2028 or early 2029 (ESA).
On 5 July 2026, JAXA's Hayabusa2 passed about 400 m above asteroid Torifune, the closest flyby of any Solar System body so far (JAXA).
ESA's Hera arrives at the asteroid Dimorphos in November 2026 to measure what NASA's DART impact did, turning deflection into a repeatable defense.
NASA's Lucy is touring asteroids; after Dinkinesh and Donaldjohanson, it reaches its first Trojan asteroid, Eurybates, on 11 August 2027 (NASA).
NASA NEO Surveyor is the first space telescope built to find hazardous asteroids, including dark ones hidden in the Sun's glare. Launch NET September 2027.
On April 13, 2029, asteroid Apophis passes about 20,000 miles from Earth. NASA's OSIRIS-APEX meets it in June 2029 to see how that close pass changes it.
ESA and JAXA's Ramses must launch by spring 2028 to meet Apophis before its 2029 Earth pass. Its €81.2 million build contract was signed in February 2026.
How the James Webb Space Telescope tracked asteroid 2024 YR4 in February 2026 and ruled out a 2032 Moon impact, two years before ground telescopes could.

facts.x: Comet Interceptor launches before its comet is even discovered, then waits in space to catch it.
facts.sn: ESA, Comet Interceptor factsheet

facts.x: Hayabusa2 passed just 400 m above asteroid Torifune at about 5 km per second.
facts.sn: JAXA, Hayabusa2 sets a new record for closest flyby

facts.x: NASA's Lucy will visit Trojan asteroids, leftovers from when the planets formed.
facts.sn: NASA Science, Lucy

facts.x: On April 13, 2029, asteroid Apophis will pass about 20,000 miles from Earth, closer than many geosynchronous satellites.
facts.sn: NASA, Asteroid Apophis

Project-Rawane.html.name: Project Rawane
Project-Rawane.html.blurb: Earth and space help each other. Taking care of one helps take care of the other.

sols.d: Artemis II carried four astronauts around the Moon in April 2026, reaching 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans before.
After eight years in space, BepiColombo enters orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026, the first mission to put two spacecraft there (ESA).
ESA's EnVision will study Venus from its inner core to its upper atmosphere; launch is planned for November 2031 (ESA).
NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft will study how the solar wind strips Mars' atmosphere, after an Earth slingshot in fall 2026.
Europe's first Mars rover, Rosalind Franklin, will drill 2 meters down to look for signs of past life, targeting launch in 2028.
A Brine Processor Assembly that squeezes the last water out of urine brine, lifting total water recovery to 98%.
NASA's Roman telescope launched Aug 30, 2026 to L2: Hubble-sharp images 100x wider, a census of planetary systems, first images by early 2027.
ESA's Plato will use 26 cameras to hunt for Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars, with launch planned for March 2027 on Ariane 6.
NASA's Psyche used a Mars flyby on 15 May 2026 to head for a metal-rich asteroid it will orbit from August 2029 (NASA).
Launched 11 March 2025, NASA's SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colors and finished its first all-sky map in 2025 (NASA JPL).
NASA's Veggie garden grows fresh food on the International Space Station; in 2015 astronauts ate the first lettuce grown in it (NASA).

Rivers.html.name: Rivers
Rivers.html.blurb: Rivers carry water from the land to the sea. Trash catchers and dam removals help fish swim home again.

sols.d: American Rivers has worked directly on more than 200 dam removals; in 2025 the U.S.
In Oregon's Bridge Creek, beavers given simple dam starters raised juvenile steelhead survival 52% and production 175% (NOAA Fisheries).
The removal of the Elwha and Glines Canyon dams so the river could flow free from the mountains to the sea.
FreshWater Watch trains citizen scientists to test rivers, lakes and ponds: 80,000+ datasets from 22,000+ volunteers (organization figures).
Four Klamath River dams came out by October 2024, reopening more than 400 miles of habitat to salmon, steelhead and lamprey (Klamath River Renewal).
A barge-based river cleanup crew that, with more than 141,000 volunteers, has pulled over 14 million pounds of trash from U.S.
Baltimore's Trash Wheels intercept about 500 tons of trash a year before it reaches the harbor and the Chesapeake Bay (organization figure).
Cleanup events, waste recovery on polluted rivers and education to stop plastic at the source.
Trash barriers and daily cleanups stopping plastic in Indonesian rivers. Barriers, daily cleanups, and sorting on Indonesia’s rivers.
A curtain of bubbles catching plastic across the full width and depth of a waterway.

Space.html.name: Space
Space.html.blurb: Space is part of our home too. People are learning to keep it clean and to use the Sun’s power up there.

sols.d: Astroscale inspects, services and removes debris in orbit: ELSA-d, ADRAS-J's 2024 close-up of an H-IIA upper stage, and ADRAS-J2, targeted for fiscal 2027.
ClearSpace leads Europe's first active debris removal mission and provides in-orbit servicing.
Globe at Night invites anyone to measure how dark their night sky is. People have sent 331,065 observations to track light pollution (program figures).
Jupiter is a natural space debris removal system that swallows or flings away far more dangerous objects than any human mission could.
Compute in orbit: solar power, radiative cooling, and no water-cooling towers. AI chips in orbit, powered by the sun and cooled by space itself.

facts.x: Anyone with a phone and a dark-adapted pair of eyes can help measure light pollution for Globe at Night.

Space_Disposal.html.name: Space Disposal
Space_Disposal.html.blurb: Old satellites and broken bits are space junk. New missions are learning to grab them and clean up orbit.

sols.d: ESA guided its retired Aeolus wind satellite down in the first assisted reentry of its kind, cutting the already low debris risk by a factor of 150.
A natural debris vacuum. Even where the air is extremely thin, it still produces drag that slows objects in low Earth orbit and pulls them down until they burn up.
NASA's Europa Clipper is on its way to Jupiter's ocean moon, with an Earth gravity assist on December 3, 2026 and 49 close Europa flybys from 2030.
ESA's Juice will study Ganymede, Callisto and Europa, with 35 moon flybys after it reaches Jupiter in July 2031. Cruising.
A global network of ground-based radars that track satellites and debris in low Earth orbit and turn the data into collision warnings, a kind of traffic camera system for low orbit.
LignoSat, the world's first wooden satellite, proved wood can survive in orbit; a follow-on is a potential solution on the horizon.
JAXA's MMX launches October 2026 to land on Mars's moon Phobos and return at least 10 grams of it to Earth in 2031, a first for the Mars system.
Life extension in GEO: two MEVs have docked with three satellites, and the Mission Robotic Vehicle and three pods launched July 21, 2026 (company figures).
PRELUDE is a ClearSpace and ESA mission planned for June 2027 to validate close-proximity rendezvous technology. A potential solution on the horizon.
The first Otter launched October 1, 2026 for NASA's SSPICY mission, inspecting up to four dead satellites and rocket bodies from 2027.
Saving moons, saving planets: the Moon keeps Earth's 23.5-degree tilt in check, which keeps our seasons and climate stable (NASA).
Titan is a prebiotic time capsule, and NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft explores it from 2034, building radar, power and autonomy tools that matter for Earth.
NASA selected SpaceX to build the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle that will guide the International Space Station safely out of orbit after 2030.
The Zero Debris Charter sets shared targets to stop creating space debris by 2030; by May 2026 it had 228 signatories from 34 countries (ESA).

terms.d: The curved path an object takes as it travels around a planet, moon or star, like a satellite circling Earth.
To bring a satellite or piece of space junk down out of orbit on purpose, usually so it burns up in the atmosphere.
When a spacecraft or piece of space junk falls back into Earth's air. The friction makes it very hot, so most small objects burn up.
A tool that sends out radio waves and listens for the echoes. From space it can see the ground through clouds, day or night.
Old satellites, rocket parts and broken pieces left in orbit that no longer do anything useful.
A greenhouse gas that traps much more heat than carbon dioxide over a few decades. It leaks from oil and gas sites, landfills and farms.
A rocky object that orbits the Sun, much smaller than a planet. Most are in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.
The total amount of living material, like the wood and leaves in a forest. Measuring it shows how much carbon plants store.
A gas, like carbon dioxide or methane, that traps heat in the air around Earth, the way a greenhouse keeps plants warm.
A kind of light our eyes can't see that we feel as heat. Special cameras use it to see warm objects and gases.

Space_Weather.html.name: Space Weather & Shields
Space_Weather.html.blurb: The Sun sends out storms of energy. Earth has invisible shields, and satellites warn us when a storm is coming.

sols.d: Aditya-L1 is ISRO's first space-based solar observatory, studying the Sun from a halo orbit around L1, about 1.5 million km from Earth.
The first mission dedicated to Earth's exosphere, Carruthers watches our planet's ultraviolet halo from about a million miles sunward.
NOAA's GOES-19 carries CCOR-1, the world's first operational space-based coronagraph, imaging the Sun's corona every 15 minutes.
NASA's IMAP watches the Sun from about a million miles sunward and can give about a half hour's warning of incoming radiation.
Four suitcase-sized NASA satellites image the Sun's corona and solar wind together, in 3D, since March 2025. Active in low Earth orbit.
ESA and NASA's Solar Orbiter took the first close-up images of the Sun's poles, coming within 42 million km of the Sun. Active, orbiting the Sun.
NOAA's SOLAR-1 (formerly SWFO-L1) watches the Sun from L1, about one million miles from Earth, streaming space weather data to forecasters in real time.
Three natural shields protect Earth: the heliosphere, the magnetosphere, and the atmosphere and ozone layer.
NASA's twin TRACERS satellites fly through Earth's polar cusps to study magnetic reconnection, a key driver of space weather.
ESA's Vigil will watch the Sun from L5, giving up to four to five days' notice of certain space weather effects. Launch is planned for 2031.

facts.x: Earth wears a faint ultraviolet halo, the geocorona, first photographed from the Moon by Apollo 16 in 1972; NASA's Carruthers mission now charts it from a million miles away.
facts.sn: NASA, Carruthers Geocorona Observatory

facts.x: GOES-19's CCOR-1 is the world's first operational space-based coronagraph, imaging the Sun's faint corona every 15 minutes.
facts.sn: NOAA SWPC, CCOR-1 coronagraph

facts.x: From about a million miles toward the Sun, NASA's IMAP can give astronauts and spacecraft near Earth about a half hour's warning of incoming radiation.
facts.sn: NASA, IMAP mission

terms.d: A steady stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun in every direction.
The curved path an object takes as it travels around a planet, moon or star, like a satellite circling Earth.
A gas high in the sky that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun. Near the ground, ozone is a pollutant.
Earth's invisible magnetic shield. It steers most of the Sun's charged particles away from our planet.
A spot in space where the pull of the Sun and Earth balance, so a spacecraft can stay in place with little fuel. L1 sits between Earth and the Sun.
An instrument that collects light (or other energy) to see faraway things more clearly.
A high orbit, about 22,000 miles up, where a satellite moves with Earth's spin and stays over the same spot.
